title: A Federal Judge Just Killed Trump's $100,000 H-1B Fee. Indian Tech Exhaled.
excerpt: Judge Leo Sorokin called it an unauthorized tax. Only 85 companies had paid it. The White House says it will appeal — but for now, the most punitive visa fee in US history is dead.
body:
A federal judge in Massachusetts ruled on Monday that the Trump administration's $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa petitions is unlawful, striking down what had been the most aggressive attempt to reshape skilled-worker immigration in a generation.

US District Judge Leo Sorokin, in a sweeping 62-page decision, declared the fee an unauthorized tax that violated the Administrative Procedure Act. He vacated the policy entirely — not just for the coalition of states that brought the lawsuit, but nationwide.

"There are no statutory powers authorizing Defendants to implement a $100,000 tax on H-1B petitions," Sorokin wrote. "The Court finds that the Policy imposes a tax on H-1B petitions without the requisite delegation by Congress."

## How the Fee Transformed the Visa Landscape

President Trump introduced the $100,000 surcharge last September, arguing the H-1B program was "fueling the large-scale replacement of American workers." Before the proclamation, employers typically paid between $2,000 and $5,000 in total fees per application. The tenfold-plus increase was designed to be prohibitive — and it worked.

As of February 15, US Citizenship and Immigration Services had received just 85 payments of the $100,000 fee, totalling $8.5 million. That number tells the real story: the fee didn't generate revenue so much as it froze the pipeline.

The states that challenged the policy — led by Massachusetts — argued the fee devastated their ability to staff publicly run hospitals, universities, and school systems. Healthcare networks that relied on foreign-trained doctors and specialists found themselves unable to bring workers in at the new price point.

## What This Means for Indian Workers and IT Firms

The H-1B program issues 65,000 visas annually, with an additional 20,000 reserved for workers with advanced degrees. Indian nationals receive a disproportionate share — roughly 72% of all H-1B approvals in recent years.

Indian IT services companies, from Infosys to TCS, rely on the program to rotate engineers and consultants to client sites in the US. And the largest American technology companies are equally dependent: Amazon received 19,301 H-1B approvals between 2024 and mid-2025, followed by Microsoft with 9,914 and Apple with 8,075. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Nvidia have all ramped up applications amid the AI talent war.

Indian equity markets reacted swiftly. IT stocks, which had been under pressure from fears that the fee would slow revenue growth in their largest market, were flagged as a key sector to watch on Tuesday's trading session. The Nifty 50 opened higher after the ruling, with IT and banking stocks leading the rebound.

## The Appeal Battle Ahead

The ruling is not the final word. White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said the administration was "confident this order will be reversed on appeal," noting that a federal judge in Washington had upheld a "nearly identical order" in a separate challenge brought by the US Chamber of Commerce.

That creates a circuit split — two federal courts reaching opposite conclusions on the same policy — which could eventually push the issue to the Supreme Court.

The fee does not apply to renewals or to foreign citizens already in the US on student visas who are converting to H-1B status. That exemption spared a large cohort of Indian-origin graduates at American universities, who make up a significant share of new H-1B recipients each year.

## The Bigger Picture

For the roughly 900,000 Indians currently on H-1B visas or in the queue, the ruling removes an immediate financial threat. But it does not resolve the deeper structural problems in the system — the decades-long green card backlog, the annual cap that leaves hundreds of thousands of qualified applicants in limbo, and the EB-2 India queue that just moved backward by ten months.

The H-1B program has become the terrain on which broader debates about immigration, economic competitiveness, and the future of the American tech workforce are being fought. Monday's ruling was a reprieve, not a resolution.
